periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Before-Reading: Soldiers, Bravery, and the Republic Day Parade

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Pairs discuss Republic Day parade and bravery awards
Groups discuss qualities a soldier should have

phases.description: Teacher opens with a brief show of a Republic Day visual and invites students to share what they know about 26 January celebrations. Pairs discuss the parade highlights and bravery awards given on the day.
Groups of four brainstorm qualities a soldier should have and frame a short message they would send to a soldier. Groups share aloud; teacher records key qualities on the board.
Teacher introduces the chapter title and previews the story of Major Somnath Sharma, connecting the discussed soldier qualities to his profile. Students predict what the section will cover.
Wrap-up: students note two new words they expect to encounter in a story about a battle and share with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: This period activates prior knowledge before the prose reading begins; the transition into Period 2 will be the first reading of the text. Students may be unfamiliar with the 1947 Indo-Pakistan conflict — a brief contextual statement (Operation Gulmarg aimed at capturing Srinagar airport) will help comprehension without spoiling the narrative.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Chronological Ordering and Extract Analysis — Battle at Badgam

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Arrange key events in chronological order
Extract 1: MCQ and inference questions on battle

homework.task_brief: Extract 2 questions on early life — self-study

phases.description: Teacher briefly recaps Period 1 discussion and situates today's reading in the timeline of the 1947 conflict. Students open textbooks to the prose section.

Students read the chronological ordering activity for the Let us discuss section — eight events from Sharma's birth to the posthumous PVC award. Pairs compare answers and teacher discusses the correct sequence.

Teacher reads Extract 1 aloud ('The air was thick with gunfire…'). Class works through the MCQ on battlefield conditions, the sentence-completion on Sharma's continued leadership, the Assertion-Reason MCQ, and the fill-in-the-blank on what Sharma did despite injuries.
Quick class debrief: teacher asks one student to summarise what Extract 1 tells us about Major Sharma's character. Homework for Extract 2 is assigned.

periods.teacher_notes: The Assertion-Reason format in Extract 1 is likely new to many Grade VIII students; briefly explain the four answer options before they attempt it. Extract 2 (early life, family heritage) is assigned as homework so class time is reserved for the richer discussion questions in Period 3.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Reflective Discussion on Legacy and Listening: Param Vir Chakra

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Discuss Sharma's legacy, last words, and leadership significance
Listen to PVC talk; complete fill-in-the-blank sentences

phases.description: Teacher checks homework on Extract 2 by cold-calling two students for answers, briefly affirming or correcting.

Class discussion on selected questions from Let us think and reflect Part II — specifically Sharma's last words ('I shall not withdraw an inch…'), the significance of repetition in 'forever alive, forever alive', and why his leadership was critical at Badgam. Teacher facilitates, inviting multiple student voices.

Listening activity: teacher reads the Param Vir Chakra transcript aloud (p.98) twice at natural pace. Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank sentences about the PVC's meaning, institution, designer, and design details.
Pair-check of listening answers; teacher confirms correct responses.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript (p.98) is short and factual; two readings at a natural pace are sufficient. Period 4 will move to speaking and writing, so keep the RFC discussion focused on the most significant ECR questions rather than all six.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Nation Service Speech and Formal Letter of Enquiry

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Groups speak on serving the nation using theme prompts
Write formal letter of enquiry to memorial incharge

phases.description: Teacher connects the prior discussion on Sharma's sacrifice to the speaking theme: 'As citizens, how do we serve our nation today?' The four theme options are written on the board.

Groups of four to five choose a theme (saving the environment / health and well-being / helping others / righteous conduct) and prepare a two-minute group speech using the sentence prompts. Each group nominates one speaker; two groups present.

Teacher introduces the letter of enquiry format: purpose, layout, tone, and required information points (visit dates, tour duration, entry fees, student group guidelines). A sample opening line is modelled on the board.

Students draft their formal letter of enquiry to a memorial incharge independently, following the layout provided in the textbook. Teacher circulates and gives formative feedback on format and register.
Students underline one sentence in their letter that they think best demonstrates formal register; one volunteer reads their sentence aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Speaking groups should be reminded to use the sentence prompts as a scaffold, not a script — natural expression is the goal. For the writing task, watch for common errors: informal salutations, missing subject line, and mixing first-person and third-person register.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Battlefield Vocabulary, Collective Nouns, and Subject-Verb Agreement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Match idiomatic expressions; complete sentences with idioms
Match collective nouns for armed forces; fill blanks
Subject-verb agreement: fill blanks and correct passage

homework.task_brief: Over- prefix verbs: definitions and own sentences

phases.description: Teacher recaps the Battle of Badgam context and explains that today's language work draws directly from the prose section's military vocabulary and grammar.

Students work individually on the idiom matching task (fight to the last man / foil the plan / deliver a blow / hold their ground) then complete the four sentences using those idioms. Pairs compare answers; class confirms.
Collective nouns activity: teacher elicits meanings of regiment, squadron, fleet, battalion before students match and fill blanks. Students discuss which term fits each armed forces context.

Subject-verb agreement: teacher explains the rules briefly using two examples from the text. Students fill in the ten blanks independently, then correct the military drill passage. Class review follows.

Consolidation: teacher writes three sentences on the board — one using an idiom, one with a collective noun, one testing agreement — and cold-calls students to complete them. Homework tasks on over- verbs and noun/verb pairs are assigned.

periods.teacher_notes: The subject-verb agreement passage correction (the military drill excerpt) works well as a class activity read aloud; students can identify and call out errors as the teacher writes them on the board. The over- prefix and advice/advise tasks are manageable independently at home and will reinforce the class work.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: PVC Awardees, Gallantry Awards, and Women in the Armed Forces

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Research gallantry awards and women's roles in armed forces

homework.task_brief: Read Birsa Munda passage; compile patriotic songs list

phases.description: Teacher introduces the Let us explore section: the twenty-one PVC awardees from Major Somnath Sharma to Captain Vikram Batra. Students read the passage on Captain Vikram Batra silently.

Groups of four research gallantry awards (Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra) using textbook information and share preliminary findings. Groups then discuss and note key roles of women in the Indian Armed Forces.
Groups present findings in a two-minute round-robin; teacher adds key points and notes similarities and differences between awards on the board.
Teacher previews Section B (Somebody's Mother poem) as a shift in theme from national valour to everyday human kindness. Homework on patriotic songs is assigned.

periods.teacher_notes: Section A ends here; Period 7 begins Section B. Students who found the research task engaging can be directed to the National War Memorial website for further independent reading outside class.
materials: Reference materials or library access if available

periods.activity_title: Reading and Appreciating 'Somebody's Mother' — Empathy and Poetic Devices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Before-reading: recall helping someone; word association
Arrange poem events in correct order
Fill blanks: theme, tone, rhyme scheme of poem
Identify simile, alliteration, repetition from poem

phases.description: Before-reading: students write two words each for their own feelings and the feelings of someone they once helped, then share with a partner. Teacher elicits the word-association activity (elderly person vs. school student vocabulary).

Teacher reads the full poem aloud with expression; students follow in their texts. Class briefly discusses the meaning of 'ragged' in context, selecting from the MCQ options. A shared reading of selected stanzas follows.
Pairs arrange the eight poem events in correct sequence (Let us discuss task), then compare with another pair. Class confirms the sequence collaboratively.

Students complete the fill-in-the-blank activity on the poem's theme, tone, stanza structure, and rhyme scheme (AABB). Teacher discusses why the AABB couplet structure gives the poem its ballad-like rhythm.

Students pick examples of simile ('like a flock of sheep'), alliteration ('firm and strong'), and repetition ('somebody's mother') from the poem and note them. Teacher explains the function of each device in creating empathy.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the first period on the poem; the 60-minute slot allows unhurried reading and discussion of poetic devices. The before-reading activity on personal helping experiences primes empathy, which is central to the poem's theme of shared humanity.

periods.activity_title: Imagery, Extract Analysis, and Listening to Rohan's Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Extract 1 questions: appearance, weather imagery, fact-opinion
Listen to Rohan broadcast; fill blanks with exact words

homework.task_brief: Extract 2 questions — trembling feet contrast — self-study

phases.description: Teacher briefly recaps the poem's narrative arc from Period 7 and connects to today's extract-based analysis.

Students work through Extract 1 questions (Let us think and reflect p.74): the MCQ on 'ragged and grey', the sentence completion on why the woman was 'bent', the fact-and-opinion identification task, and the ECR on 'aged and slow' feet. Teacher facilitates discussion of the winter imagery and its role in the poem.

Listening activity: teacher reads the Rohan Bahir news broadcast (p.99) aloud twice. Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank sentences on strong currents, Rohan's hesitation, onlookers, the honour at Vigyan Bhawan, and the message about age.
Quick pair-check of listening blanks. Extract 2 (contrast between trembling and firm feet) is assigned as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The fact-and-opinion distinction in Extract 1 is a key critical reading skill; ensure students understand that 'The woman was too weak to cross' is an inference/opinion, while 'The street was wet with recent snow' is a fact. The listening transcript for Section B is at p.99.

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary from the Poem and Diary Entry Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Match poem words to underlined phrases in Column 2
Match 'hand' idioms to meanings
Write diary entry about helping someone in need

phases.description: Teacher returns focus to the poem's vocabulary, noting that words like 'hastened', 'heeded', and 'stir' carry precise meanings that are key to the poem's movement and mood.

Students match the six poem words (hastened, heeded, stir, lend, piled, offered) to underlined phrases in Column 2. Pairs compare and teacher confirms with brief explanations drawn from the poem's context.

Students match the six 'hand' idioms (get out of hand, try your hand, give a free hand, give a big hand, work hand in hand, have your hands full) to their meanings and discuss how 'lend a hand' in the poem connects to the idiom set.

Teacher introduces the diary entry format: personal tone, first person, date and time header, internal reflection. Students draft a diary entry about a day they helped someone, including situation, place, feelings during and after, and reasons to repeat the act. Teacher circulates and gives formative feedback.
Students share one sentence from their diary entry that best captures their emotion. Teacher notes common strengths and one area for improvement.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary work on poem words feeds naturally into the writing task — students may draw on 'hastened', 'offered', and 'guided' when narrating their own helping incident. Watch for diary entries that sound like formal essays; prompt students toward a conversational, reflective register.

periods.activity_title: Pronunciation of '-ed' Endings, Paired Narration, and Motherland Project

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Sort '-ed' words by final sound; read aloud columns
Pairs narrate a past helping incident using cue cards
Groups find motherland and fatherland countries; make gratitude card

phases.description: Teacher explains the three pronunciations of '-ed' endings (/id/, /d/, /t/) with examples from the poem (ragged, aged, guided, whispered). Students read aloud the eight words and sort them into the correct columns in their notebooks.

Pairs narrate an incident where they helped someone, using the cue cards (at school / at the market / in the neighbourhood / in the playground) and sentence prompts. Partners take turns and provide brief feedback on clarity and fluency.

Groups of four begin the Let us explore task: locating the Sanskrit verse on Earth as mother, identifying countries that use 'motherland' versus 'fatherland', and planning a gratitude card for their mother or grandmother. Groups share country lists.
Teacher previews Section C (Verghese Kurien's letter) and connects the theme — writing to preserve wisdom across generations — to the gratitude card activity just completed.

periods.teacher_notes: The '-ed' pronunciation sorting activity works best if students read the words aloud together before categorising; silent individual work misses the oral purpose. Section B ends here; Period 11 opens Section C.
materials: Recycled card material for gratitude cards (optional)

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Reading Kurien's Letter — Facts, Opinions, and Listening to Evelyn Glennie

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Before-reading: communication timeline; pairs discuss social media
Identify facts and opinions in Kurien's letter
Listen to Evelyn Glennie passage; true/false and SCR

phases.description: Before-reading: students arrange six communication means in a timeline (carrier pigeons → telegraph → telephone → postcard → email → mobile phone). Pairs discuss preferred communication and social media benefits and precautions.

Students read Kurien's letter silently up to the point covered in the prose summary, then complete the fact-and-opinion identification task (eight statements). Pairs compare, teacher discusses the distinction between Kurien's reflections (opinions) and verifiable events (facts).

Listening: teacher reads the Evelyn Glennie passage (p.100) twice. Students complete the true/false activity (five statements on her journey) and the three short-answer questions in one or two words each. Class discusses answers.
Teacher connects Evelyn Glennie's determination to Dr. Kurien's message about failure and best effort, setting up Period 12's discussion and writing work.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript for Section C is at p.100; Evelyn Glennie's story is motivating and students often respond well to it. The fact-and-opinion task on Kurien's letter requires students to distinguish between his personal reflections and verifiable biographical events — guide them to look for hedging language as a cue.

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Vocabulary, Punctuation, and Letter to Grandparents

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Replace underlined words with synonyms from Kurien's letter
Match expressions from the text to meanings
Write letter to grandparents thanking for life lessons

phases.description: Students replace underlined words in six sentences with the correct synonym from the box (essential, swift, lifelong, momentary, useful, splendid). Teacher highlights how each synonym appears in Kurien's letter context.

Students match six expressions from the letter (in all humility / hold their heads high / to be quite honest / to the best of your ability / looked at in awe / somewhere deep down) to their meanings. Class confirms answers; teacher notes how these phrases reflect Kurien's values of integrity and service.

Students write a personal letter to their grandparents, inspired by Kurien's letter format, thanking them for life lessons and explaining how those lessons inspire them to contribute to society. Teacher circulates and offers brief individual feedback.

Closing reflection: teacher asks two volunteers to read one sentence from their letters. Chapter is rounded off with a brief connect across all three sections — valour, kindness, and service as expressions of values and dispositions.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task echoes Kurien's letter structure — personal, warm, and purposeful. Students who struggle to start may be reminded that Kurien opens by contrasting phone calls with the lasting joy of written letters, and they can begin similarly. Remaining vocabulary tasks (em dash/en dash, contractions, prepositional phrases) are available as self-study for interested students.

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student analyses Major Somnath Sharma's leadership, last words, and the Battle of Badgam using chronological ordering, extract-based inference, and reflective discussion drawn from the prose section.
items.item_stem:
When an enemy force of roughly 500 soldiers attacked D Company at Badgam, Major Somnath Sharma was ordered to withdraw but refused. Read the account of his final hours and answer the questions below.

(a) What did Major Sharma do when ordered to withdraw from Badgam, and what reason did he give?
(b) Even though D Company was overrun after his death, how did Sharma's decision to hold ground ultimately benefit India?
(c) What do Sharma's actions — calling for air strikes, laying ground panels, filling ammunition magazines under fire — reveal about the kind of leader he was?

expected_elements: Sharma refused withdrawal, citing 50-yard enemy distance and resolve to fight to the last round.
His men held for six more hours, buying time for reinforcements to save Srinagar.
Actions show hands-on, fearless leadership that motivated soldiers under devastating fire.
Response links personal sacrifice to the larger strategic outcome for India.

items.source_lo: Student identifies the poem's theme, tone, rhyme scheme, poetic devices, and central imagery of empathy and shared humanity as expressed through the narrative of the old woman and the boy.
items.item_stem:
In 'Somebody's Mother' by Mary Dow Brine, a crowd of jubilant schoolboys passes an elderly woman stranded at a snowy crossing without offering help, until one boy pauses.

Read the stanza below and answer the questions that follow:

'She's somebody's mother, boys, you know,
For all she's aged and poor and slow,
And I hope some fellow will lend a hand
To help my mother, you understand,
If ever she's poor and old and grey,
When her own dear boy is far away.'

(a) What is the central theme of the poem, and how does the boy's reasoning in this stanza express it?
(b) The poem follows an AABB rhyme scheme in couplets. Identify ONE couplet from the stanza above and explain how the rhyme contributes to the poem's gentle, ballad-like tone.
(c) Identify the poetic device used in the line 'Came the boys like a flock of sheep' and explain its effect.

expected_elements: Central theme is kindness and empathy; the boy sees the woman as someone's loved one.
One AABB couplet identified (e.g., know/slow or hand/understand); rhyme gives gentle, flowing rhythm.
Simile 'like a flock of sheep' compares the boys to a mindless, indifferent group.
Response explains how the poem moves from indifference to compassion through the boy's insight.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student distinguishes facts from opinions in Dr. Kurien's letter and identifies key ideas about service, integrity, and communication using the textual content of the letter.
items.item_stem:
Dr. Verghese Kurien's letter to his grandson Siddharth includes both verifiable facts and personal opinions.

Read the statements below and write F (Fact) or O (Opinion) for each. Then choose ONE opinion statement and explain in two sentences what it reveals about Dr. Kurien's values.

1. Dr. Kurien started his working life soon after India became independent.
2. Speaking on the telephone gives only an immediate but fleeting joy.
3. Dr. Kurien worked for a small dairy cooperative in Anand, Gujarat.
4. Failure is not about not succeeding but about not putting in one's best effort.
5. Dr. Kurien received the Padma Vibhushan in 1999.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1-F, 2-O, 3-F, 4-O, 5-F. Accept any opinion statement (2 or 4); an adequate explanation links the chosen opinion to Kurien's belief in integrity, hard work, or the enduring value of written communication over transient phone calls.

items.item_stem:
Listen to the talk about the Param Vir Chakra and fill in each blank with the exact word or phrase you hear.

1. The Param Vir Chakra is awarded for exemplary bravery shown in the presence of the ________.
2. The medal was instituted with retrospective effect from 15 August 1947 by ________, the then President of India.
3. The designer of the Param Vir Chakra was ________, who drew inspiration from a Vedic rishi.
4. The Param Vir Chakra is cast in ________.
5. On the medal, the State Emblem is surrounded by four replicas of Indra's Vajra lined with ________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. enemy. 2. Dr. Rajendra Prasad. 3. Mrs. Savitri Khanolkar. 4. bronze. 5. lotus flowers.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a news broadcast about Rohan Bahir's act of courage and completes sentences with exact words about the river rescue and the Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the news broadcast and fill in each blank with one to three exact words you hear.

1. Rohan saved a woman who had fallen into the ________ River while washing clothes.
2. The woman was struggling to stay afloat because of the ________.
3. Rohan leapt into the river without a moment's ________.
4. Rohan was honoured at ________ with the Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar 2023.
5. The broadcast concludes that age is no ________ when it comes to saving lives.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Domri. 2. strong currents. 3. hesitation. 4. Vigyan Bhawan. 5. barrier.

Listen to the passage about Evelyn Glennie and state whether each sentence below is True or False. Write T or F.

1. Evelyn Glennie lost her hearing suddenly, all at once.
2. Ron Forbes was a percussionist who recognised Evelyn's potential.
3. Evelyn learned to sense music through the vibrations felt in different parts of her body.
4. Her school performance improved steadily before her hearing loss was discovered.
5. Evelyn eventually became one of the world's most sought-after multi-percussionists.

options.text: Evelyn Glennie lost her hearing suddenly, all at once.
Ron Forbes was a percussionist who recognised Evelyn's potential.
Evelyn learned to sense music through the vibrations felt in different parts of her body.
Her school performance improved steadily before her hearing loss was discovered.
Evelyn eventually became one of the world's most sought-after multi-percussionists.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1-F (her hearing loss was gradual, not sudden). 2-T. 3-T (she felt higher drum from the waist up and lower from the waist down). 4-F (her school performance deteriorated). 5-T.

items.source_lo: Student speaks in a group about ways to serve the nation, organising ideas around a chosen theme using sentence prompts for fluency and coherence.
items.item_stem:
Major Somnath Sharma gave his life in service to the nation. Think about the ways in which ordinary citizens — including students — can serve their country today.

In your group, prepare and deliver a two-minute speech on ONE of the following themes: Saving the Environment / Health and Well-being / Helping Others / Righteous Conduct.

Your speech should: state the theme clearly, give at least two specific actions citizens can take, explain why these actions matter for the nation, and end with a call to action for your audience.

expected_elements: States chosen theme clearly at the opening.
Gives at least two specific, realistic citizen actions.
Explains connection between the actions and national well-being.
Delivers a clear closing call to action for the audience.

items.source_lo: Student writes a reflective diary entry about a day spent helping someone in need, incorporating personal feelings, the situation, and reasons to repeat the act in an appropriate diary format.
items.item_stem:
The boy in 'Somebody's Mother' helped an elderly woman cross a snowy street and returned to his friends with his 'young heart happy and well content.'

Inspired by this act of kindness, write a diary entry (130–160 words) about a day you helped someone in need. Your diary entry should include:
- The date, time, and a suitable opening line.
- A description of who you helped and the situation.
- What you did to help and how the person responded.
- Your feelings during the act and afterwards.
- A brief reflection on why you would choose to help again.

Begin your entry with: '________, ________ p.m. Dear Diary, Today felt like a day that truly mattered…'

expected_elements: Diary format observed: date, time, personal salutation, and suitable opening.
Situation, action, and the other person's reaction described with specific detail.
Personal feelings during and after the act expressed clearly and authentically.
Closing reflection explains motivation or willingness to help again.

items.source_lo: Student writes a personal letter to grandparents acknowledging life lessons and connecting those lessons to a commitment to contribute to society, modelled on Dr. Kurien's letter style.
items.item_stem:
Dr. Verghese Kurien wrote a long letter to his grandson Siddharth from Anand, Gujarat in 2005, sharing the values of integrity, humility, and service that guided his life. He believed written letters carry an enduring joy that telephone calls cannot.

Write a personal letter (150–180 words) to your grandparents thanking them for the lessons they have taught you. Your letter should:
- Open warmly and mention one specific lesson or story you have learned from them.
- Explain how their example of helping others or living with integrity has shaped your values.
- Describe one concrete way their actions inspire you to contribute to your community or society.
- Close with a heartfelt expression of gratitude.

expected_elements: Warm, personal tone consistent with a letter to a family elder.
At least one specific lesson, story, or example from the grandparents named.
Clear connection drawn between grandparents' values and own behaviour or aspirations.
One concrete action or contribution to community described.

items.item_stem:
The prose account of the Battle of Badgam uses specialised military vocabulary and precise grammar. Complete each task below.

Part A — Collective Nouns: Fill in the blank with the correct collective noun for armed forces (regiment / squadron / battalion / fleet).
1. The admiral ordered the entire ________ of warships to advance toward the coastline.
2. A ________ of infantry soldiers was positioned at the edge of the forest before the attack.
3. The ________ of fighter aircraft intercepted the enemy before dawn.

Part B — Subject-Verb Agreement: Choose the correct verb from the brackets.
1. Each of the soldiers ________ (was / were) trained to hold ground under heavy fire.
2. The battalion of Kumaon Regiment soldiers ________ (fights / fight) with extraordinary valour.
3. Neither the commander nor his men ________ (was / were) willing to retreat.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Part A: 1. fleet. 2. battalion. 3. squadron. Part B: 1. was. 2. fights. 3. were.

items.item_stem:
Dr. Kurien's letter to his grandson uses precise and expressive language. Complete both tasks below.

1. The ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan was a magnificent occasion that none of us will forget.
2. Dr. Kurien experienced a fleeting sense of doubt before committing fully to the cooperative in Anand.
3. His dedication to the farmers of India was an abiding commitment that lasted until the end of his life.

Part B — Expressions: Match the expression from Kurien's letter with its meaning.
1. in all humility     (a) speak truthfully without pretence
2. to be quite honest     (b) being modest with no sense of self-importance
3. hold their heads high     (c) feel and show dignified pride and confidence

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Part A: 1. splendid. 2. momentary. 3. lifelong. Part B: 1-b. 2-a. 3-c.

items.source_lo: Student researches gallantry awards and the roles of women in the Indian Armed Forces, connecting findings to the context of PVC awardees discussed in the Let us explore section.
items.item_stem:
The Let us explore section in your textbook profiles twenty-one Param Vir Chakra awardees from Major Somnath Sharma (the first, 1947) to Captain Vikram Batra (the last, 1999). It also discusses the growing role of women in India's armed forces.

In your group, carry out the following project and prepare a brief presentation (3–4 minutes) for the class:

(a) List the three highest gallantry awards given by the Government of India (Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra). For each award, note: who may receive it, what criteria must be met, and what the medal looks like.
(b) Find out two key roles that women currently serve in the Indian Army, Navy, or Air Force.
(c) State what connects the spirit of Major Somnath Sharma's sacrifice to the roles women play in the armed forces today.

expected_elements: Accurate description of all three gallantry awards with recipient criteria.
At least two verified roles for women in the Indian Armed Forces named.
Presentation is structured with a clear opening, body, and conclusion.
Connection drawn between Sharma's values and contemporary military service.

items.source_lo: Student investigates cultural concepts of motherland and fatherland across countries and creates a gratitude card for a mother or grandmother, connecting to the poem's theme of maternal bonds.
items.item_stem:
The poem 'Somebody's Mother' celebrates the universal bond between a mother and her child, and the Let us explore section connects this idea to how nations themselves are called 'motherland' or 'fatherland' in different cultures. The Sanskrit verse from the Atharva Veda, 'माता भूमि: पुत्रोऽहं पृथिव्या:', means 'The Earth is my mother; I am her son.'

Complete the following project:

(a) With your group, identify at least four countries that refer to their nation as 'motherland' and at least two that call it 'fatherland'. Note what cultural or historical reasons might explain the difference.
(b) Create a gratitude card for your mother or grandmother using recycled material. The card must include: at least five things she does for you, two things you commit to doing regularly to help her, and one line inspired by the poem's theme of caring for the elderly.

expected_elements: At least four motherland countries and two fatherland countries correctly identified.
Brief cultural or historical reasoning offered for the distinction.
Gratitude card includes five specific acts of care and two personal commitments.
One line in the card reflects the poem's theme of empathy toward the elderly.
